title: Measure query count and batch related reads
sources: Python 3.14 documentation: sqlite3 Connection.execute and parameter substitution
SQLite documentation: SQL Language Expressions, IN and NOT IN operators
masterChecklist: ORM concepts, migrations, query performance, N+1 query problem
Database transaction boundaries and query safety
whyItMatters: A page that queries progress once for every lesson may work on a tiny sample but slow down as the lesson list grows. Measuring the number and shape of queries points to the real cause.
simpleExplanation: N+1 means one list query followed by one related query per item. First count the queries. Then fetch related rows in one parameterized batch or join when the data and access rules permit it. Keep the empty-list case explicit so behavior is clear across database engines; SQLite permits IN (), while many other engines do not.
mentalModel: Instead of visiting the records room separately for every lesson, bring a single list of IDs and collect the matching records in one trip.
outcomes: Identify an N+1 loop in code.
Build a parameterized batched IN query from a trusted item count.
Handle an empty input without invalid SQL.

realWorldExample.scenario: The study dashboard shows completion status beside 50 lessons.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: One list query plus 50 status queries adds latency and load.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Count queries for the route, batch the permitted lesson IDs, return a dictionary keyed by ID, and test missing and empty cases.

explanation: The empty-list guard gives a clear no-query result and avoids an empty IN list when porting to an engine that disallows it.
Only the trusted number of placeholders is inserted into the SQL text; lesson ID values remain bound parameters.
One SELECT fetches all requested statuses and converts two-column rows to a dictionary.
The caller must define what a missing ID means because absent rows do not appear in the result.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Request one missing ID and observe that it is absent from the result; decide whether the dashboard should display unknown or incomplete.

procedure: Count actual database calls made by the page or job.
Check authorization before deciding which IDs can be requested.
Return immediately for an empty list.
Generate placeholders from the count, bind the values, and fetch related rows in one batch.
Measure the new query count and inspect a representative query plan when performance still matters.
Test missing IDs, duplicate IDs, and large enough batches for the application's limits.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming an ORM prevents N+1 automatically.
commonMistakes.why: Accessing related records inside a loop may still issue one query per object.
commonMistakes.avoid: Inspect actual query count and configure a deliberate batched or joined fetch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pasting IDs into the SQL string.
commonMistakes.why: Input data can change SQL syntax.
commonMistakes.avoid: Build only placeholder punctuation and bind every value separately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating fewer queries as automatically faster.
commonMistakes.why: Very large result sets, indexes, and network costs also matter.
commonMistakes.avoid: Measure representative end-to-end performance and inspect query shape.

lab.title: Batch fictional progress lookups
lab.safety: The lab uses a disposable in-memory SQLite database and fictional lesson IDs.
lab.starterCode:

guidedSteps: Create one ? for each ID and join them with commas.
Execute one SELECT with lesson_ids as the parameter sequence.
Turn the two-column rows into a dictionary.
checks: An empty list returns {} without a query.
Two IDs are fetched by one SELECT.
ID values are bound parameters rather than interpolated into SQL.
Missing IDs do not cause an exception.
hints: Build marks with `', '.join('?' for _ in lesson_ids)`.
lab.solutionExplanation: The function builds SQL punctuation from the count of values and binds actual IDs separately. It preserves a clear empty-input rule and returns only matching rows.
challenges: Define and test a policy for an ID that is missing from the database.
Count the queries used by a per-ID loop and compare them with this batch.
lab.testCode:
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing
with closing(sqlite3.connect(':memory:')) as db:
    db.execute('CREATE TABLE progress(lesson TEXT,done INTEGER)')
    db.executemany('INSERT INTO progress VALUES (?,?)',[('loops',1),('files',0)])
    assert read_status(db,['loops','files'])=={'loops':1,'files':0}
    assert read_status(db,[])=={}
print('PASS: batched progress read')

projectConnection.milestone: Replace one-progress-query-per-lesson with a measured batched read.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: A test verifies result correctness and query count for an empty list, several IDs, and a missing ID.

assessment.question: What makes a related-data loop N+1?
assessment.answer: One initial list query is followed by one query for each listed item.
assessment.explanation: Query count grows with the number of items.

assessment.question: What belongs in the SQL string for a batched IN clause?
assessment.answer: A trusted number of placeholders; values are bound separately.

assessment.question: Why handle an empty ID list first?
assessment.answer: To return an explicit empty result without a query and avoid dialect-specific empty-IN behavior.
assessment.explanation: SQLite allows IN (), but many other database engines do not.
